messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tane Faleolo is a 48-year-old Samoan-American man who works as a roofer in the Pacific Northwest. He has been married for nineteen years and, by most outward measures, has built a steady and respectable life. He came to the clinic quietly, almost reluctantly, after his wife told him she no longer recognised the man she had married. That conversation, more than anything, was what finally moved him through the door.

The assault occurred approximately two years ago. Tane had attended a trade industry gathering — an informal end-of-season get-together at a colleague's property. He had been drinking, as most of the men there had, and at some point in the evening he was separated from the group. A man he knew professionally — someone he had trusted and worked alongside — assaulted him in a back room while others remained oblivious outside. There was the smell of alcohol on the man's breath, close and insistent. There was the sound of a motorcycle idling somewhere in the driveway, its engine cutting in and out. Tane did not report the assault. He told no one. He drove home, showered, and went to work the following Monday.

For the first several months, he managed through sheer forward motion. He took on more jobs, longer days, climbed more rooftops than his body reasonably asked of him. But the memories did not behave the way he expected memories to behave. They did not fade with time. Instead, they arrived with an almost physical weight — more textured and immediate than anything else in his life, more real than his daughter's birthday or the morning light on his wife's face. He began to notice that certain things reliably pulled him back: a news segment about sexual violence, a motorcycle passing on the street below a job site, the smell of beer at a family barbecue. Each of these could return him, without warning, to that room — or worse, could flood him with the full emotional force of what happened without producing any clear image at all, just a wave of something he could not name but could not withstand. When he did allow himself to remember more directly, what came was not rage or fear but an overwhelming grief that he found almost impossible to explain, even to himself.

Tane's work as a roofer had always involved physical exertion — hauling materials, balancing on pitched surfaces in all weather — and he began to find that the physical strain of the job activated something he could not tolerate. The racing heart, the muscle tension, the breathlessness of hard labour had come to feel intolerable in ways he could not articulate to his crew. He started delegating the heaviest lifts, taking more breaks than he ever had, sometimes finding reasons to stay at ground level. His men noticed. He noticed them noticing. He said nothing.

At home, he had taken to controlling his meals with a precision that puzzled his wife. He ate small, specific portions at specific times, and he declined food at gatherings where he had no control over what was being served. He understood, on some level, that this was about more than food — that what he was seeking was the feeling that at least one thing in his body was subject to his authority. He kept himself occupied in the evenings with projects, repairs around the house, anything that prevented him from sitting still with his own thoughts. He had come to believe that stillness was dangerous, that if he stopped moving, something would catch up with him that he was not equipped to face.

His wife had tried, gently and then less gently, to reach him. He had not been able to explain what was wrong, partly because he had no language for it and partly because he was certain that telling her would change the way she saw him in ways that could not be undone. What he hoped for, sitting across from the clinician at intake, was that there might be a way to carry this that did not cost him everything he had built. What he feared most was that it was already too late for that.
